skill: Sample statistics and margin of error
stem: In a random sample of 80 voters in a city, 52 support a proposal. What percent of the sample supports the proposal?
steps: Fraction supporting: 52 ÷ 80 = 0.65.
Convert to a percent: 0.65 × 100 = 65%.
key: Sample percent = part ÷ sample size × 100.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

skill: Sample statistics and margin of error
stem: A survey of a random sample of residents estimates that 62% of residents support building a new park, with a margin of error of 4 percentage points. Which of the following is a plausible value for the percentage of all residents who support the park?
steps: The plausible range is 62% ± 4%, which is 58% to 66%.
Only 60% lies within that range.
55%, 67% and 70% fall outside it.
key: Estimate ± margin of error gives the range of plausible values.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

skill: Sample statistics and margin of error
stem: Two random samples are taken from the same population to estimate the mean height. Sample A has 100 people and sample B has 900 people. Which statement is most likely true?
choices: The margin of error for sample B is smaller than for sample A.
The margin of error for sample A is smaller than for sample B.
The two samples have the same margin of error.
Sample B's estimate must equal the true population mean.
steps: Margin of error depends on sample size: larger random samples give more precise estimates.
Sample B is 9 times larger, so its margin of error is smaller (about one-third as large).
No sample, however large, guarantees the exact population value.
key: Bigger random sample → smaller margin of error, but never zero.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

skill: Sample statistics and margin of error
stem: A random sample of 400 seniors at one high school found a mean study time of 6.2 hours per week, with a margin of error of 0.5 hours. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
choices: It is plausible that the mean study time of all seniors at that school is between 5.7 and 6.7 hours per week.
The mean study time of all high school seniors in the country is between 5.7 and 6.7 hours per week.
Every senior at the school studies between 5.7 and 6.7 hours per week.
The mean study time of all seniors at the school is exactly 6.2 hours per week.
steps: The range is 6.2 ± 0.5, which is 5.7 to 6.7 hours.
The sample came from one school, so conclusions apply only to that school's seniors, not the whole country.
The margin of error describes the mean, not every individual student.
The true mean is estimated, not known exactly.
key: Generalize only to the population sampled, and only about the parameter estimated.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

stem: Which of the following describes an experiment rather than an observational study?
choices: Researchers randomly assign 50 plants to receive fertilizer or no fertilizer, then measure their growth.
Researchers record how many hours students sleep and compare their grades.
Researchers survey shoppers about how often they buy organic food.
Researchers count birds at a lake each month for a year.
steps: In an experiment, researchers impose a treatment on the subjects.
In an observational study, researchers only measure what already happens.
Only the first choice assigns a treatment (fertilizer), and it does so randomly.
key: Experiment = researchers assign the treatment. Observational = researchers just observe.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

stem: A researcher surveys a random sample of 1,000 adults in a country and finds that coffee drinkers report fewer headaches than people who don't drink coffee. Can the researcher conclude that drinking coffee causes fewer headaches?
choices: No, because the participants were not randomly assigned to drink coffee.
Yes, because the sample is large.
Yes, because the sample was selected at random.
No, because 1,000 adults is too small a sample.
steps: Cause and effect requires random assignment to groups.
Here, people chose whether to drink coffee, so other differences between groups could explain the result.
A large random sample lets you generalize to the country's adults, but only as an association.
key: Random sampling supports generalizing; only random assignment supports causation.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

stem: Volunteers at one gym were randomly assigned to follow exercise program A or program B for 8 weeks. Those in program A lost more weight on average. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Program A likely causes more weight loss than program B for volunteers like these, but the result may not apply to all adults.
Program A causes more weight loss than program B for all adults.
The programs are only associated with weight loss; no cause can be determined.
No conclusion can be drawn because the participants were volunteers.
steps: Random assignment to programs supports a cause-and-effect conclusion.
But the participants were volunteers at one gym, not a random sample of all adults.
So the causal conclusion applies to people similar to these volunteers.
key: Random assignment → causation; who you studied limits who you can generalize to.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

stem: Researchers randomly selected 300 students from a school district and then randomly assigned half of them to receive weekly tutoring. After a semester, the tutored students had higher average test scores. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Tutoring is likely to cause higher test scores for students in the district.
Tutoring is associated with higher test scores, but no causal conclusion can be made.
Tutoring causes higher test scores for students in every district in the country.
No conclusion can be drawn about students in the district.
steps: Random selection from the district lets results generalize to the district's students.
Random assignment to tutoring supports a cause-and-effect conclusion.
With both, you can conclude tutoring likely causes higher scores for students in the district, but not beyond it.
key: Random sample + random assignment = a causal conclusion for the population sampled.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: The botanist's field notes were remarkably ______: each entry recorded the date, the soil temperature, and the exact location of every seedling.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: meticulous
hasty
ambiguous
sparse
explanation: Each entry records date, soil temperature and exact location. That level of detail describes notes that are meticulous (extremely careful and precise).
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Find the clue. After the colon the text lists what each entry recorded: the date, the soil temperature and the exact location of every seedling.
Describe the clue in your own words before looking at the choices: the notes were very detailed and careful.
Test the choices. "Meticulous" means showing great attention to detail, which matches.
Eliminate the rest. "Hasty" (rushed), "ambiguous" (unclear) and "sparse" (thin, lacking detail) all contradict the detailed list.
Answer: meticulous.
key: Words in Context: the clue after the colon defines the blank.

passage: Although the town council expected the proposal to be controversial, it received ______ support, with every member voting in favor.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: unanimous
tentative
divided
reluctant
explanation: "Every member voting in favor" means all members agreed, so the support was unanimous.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Notice the contrast word "Although": the council expected controversy, but something else happened.
Find the decisive clue: "with every member voting in favor."
Every member agreeing is the definition of "unanimous".
Eliminate: "tentative" and "reluctant" suggest hesitation; "divided" means disagreement. None fit a vote where everyone said yes.
Answer: unanimous.
key: Words in Context: an explicit fact in the sentence fixes the meaning.

passage: Monarch butterflies are often described as fragile, and individually they are: a single storm can kill thousands. Yet each autumn, millions complete a migration of up to 4,000 kilometers, guided by a time-compensated sun compass that researchers are still working to fully explain.
stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It presents a common characterization of monarch butterflies, then qualifies it by describing a remarkable capability.
It describes a scientific debate about monarch butterflies and then resolves it.
It explains a migration route and then lists the dangers along it.
It compares monarch butterflies with other migratory insects.
explanation: The text opens with the view that monarchs are fragile, agrees in part ("individually they are"), then turns with "Yet" to their 4,000-kilometer migration. That is a characterization followed by a qualification.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Sentence 1 states a common view (monarchs are fragile) and partly agrees with it ("individually they are").
Sentence 2 begins with "Yet", a turn. It describes a remarkable ability: a migration of up to 4,000 km guided by a sun compass.
So the structure is: common characterization → qualification through an impressive capability.
Check the others. There is no debate being resolved (B), no list of dangers along a route (C) and no other insects (D).
Answer: it presents a common characterization, then qualifies it.
key: Text Structure: label what each sentence does, then match the sequence.

passage: The composer's later works were initially dismissed as derivative, but critics have since come to regard their apparent simplicity as ______, the result of years of deliberate refinement rather than a lack of imagination.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: hard-won
accidental
superficial
borrowed
explanation: The text says the simplicity came from "years of deliberate refinement". Something achieved through long effort is hard-won.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: The sentence contrasts the early view ("derivative") with critics' later view.
The phrase after the blank explains it: "the result of years of deliberate refinement rather than a lack of imagination."
So the simplicity was achieved through long, careful effort.
"Hard-won" means gained through great effort. "Accidental" contradicts "deliberate"; "superficial" and "borrowed" repeat the early criticism the sentence rejects.
Answer: hard-won.
key: Words in Context: use the explanation that follows the comma.

passage:
Text 1
Some economists argue that a four-day workweek raises productivity because rested employees work more efficiently. Pilot programs at several companies reported stable or higher output after the change.

Text 2
Pilot programs of the four-day workweek have mostly involved firms that volunteered to participate, often firms whose leaders already expected the change to succeed. Such programs may say less about the policy itself than about the companies that chose to try it.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the evidence described in Text 1?
choices: By suggesting that the pilot results may reflect which firms took part rather than the effect of the policy alone
By arguing that rested employees are not more efficient than tired ones
By claiming that output at the pilot companies actually fell
By recommending that companies keep a five-day workweek
explanation: Text 2 points out that the firms volunteered and expected success. Its concern is selection: the results may describe the companies, not the policy. It never says output fell or that rest does not help.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Text 1's evidence: pilot programs showed stable or higher output after a four-day week.
Text 2's point: the firms volunteered, and their leaders already expected success.
That is a selection problem. The good results might come from the kind of company that joined, not from the policy itself.
Eliminate: Text 2 never says rest doesn't help (B), never says output fell (C) and never recommends a five-day week (D).
Answer: the results may reflect which firms participated rather than the policy alone.
key: Cross-Text: identify exactly what Text 2 doubts about Text 1's evidence.

passage: In her review, the critic did not condemn the novel outright; instead, her praise was so ______ that readers could hardly miss her reservations.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: qualified
effusive
unequivocal
spontaneous
explanation: The critic did not condemn the novel but readers could see her reservations, so the praise came with limits. Praise with reservations is qualified. "Effusive" and "unequivocal" would hide the reservations.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: The critic did not condemn the novel, so there was some praise.
But readers "could hardly miss her reservations", so the praise had limits.
Praise with limits or conditions is "qualified" praise.
"Effusive" (gushing) and "unequivocal" (without doubt) would hide reservations; "spontaneous" is about timing, not limits.
Answer: qualified.
key: Words in Context: the blank must allow "reservations" to show through.

passage: Engineers praised the new bridge design for being remarkably ______: it used far fewer materials than earlier designs while carrying heavier loads.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: efficient
ornate
fragile
temporary
steps: The clue after the colon: fewer materials, heavier loads.
Doing more with less is the definition of efficient.
"Ornate" means highly decorated; "fragile" contradicts carrying heavier loads; "temporary" is unsupported.
key: The text after a colon often defines or explains the missing word.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: Although the candidate's speech lasted nearly an hour, reviewers found it surprisingly ______, noting that it offered few specific proposals despite its length.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: insubstantial
concise
controversial
meticulous
steps: "Although" sets up a contrast with the speech's long length.
The explanation: it offered few specific proposals, so it had little real content.
"Insubstantial" means lacking substance, which fits.
"Concise" (brief) contradicts the hour-long length; "meticulous" (very detailed) contradicts "few specific proposals"; "controversial" is not supported.
key: Use both the contrast word and the explanation; the right word must fit both.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: Before electric refrigerators were common, many households kept food cold in iceboxes: wooden cabinets lined with tin or zinc and cooled by a large block of ice. In winter, workers cut ice from frozen lakes and stored it in insulated icehouses, and throughout the year it was delivered to homes.
stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how people kept food cold before electric refrigerators were common
To argue that iceboxes worked better than modern refrigerators
To describe how lakes freeze in winter
To compare the costs of different kinds of ice
steps: The text describes iceboxes and how ice was harvested, stored and delivered.
Its purpose is to explain a past method of keeping food cold.
It does not argue (B), focus on lakes freezing (C) or discuss costs (D).
key: Purpose questions ask why the author wrote the text: to explain, argue, describe or compare.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: Sea otters often float on their backs while eating. They use their chests as tables, cracking open shellfish against stones balanced there. Some otters even keep a favorite stone tucked in a loose pouch of skin under one forearm.
stem: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the overall structure of the text?
choices: It adds a detail about how otters keep the tools they use for eating.
It introduces a new topic unrelated to eating.
It contradicts the description in the second sentence.
It explains why otters float on their backs.
steps: Sentences 1 and 2 describe how otters eat, using stones as tools.
Sentence 3 adds that some otters store a favorite stone in a skin pouch.
That extends the tool-use detail, so A.
It stays on topic (not B), agrees with sentence 2 (not C), and doesn't explain floating (not D).
key: To find a sentence's function, ask how it connects to the sentence just before it.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: Early telescopes used glass lenses, which bend different colors of light by slightly different amounts, so their images were often blurred by colored fringes. To avoid this problem, Isaac Newton built a telescope that gathered light with a curved mirror instead of a lens. Because a mirror reflects all colors the same way, his design produced sharper images.
stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It identifies a problem with an early technology and then describes a solution to that problem.
It compares two scientists' competing theories about light.
It lists the steps for building a telescope at home.
It describes a scientific discovery and then explains why it was rejected.
steps: Sentence 1: a problem (lenses create colored fringes).
Sentence 2: a response (Newton used a mirror instead).
Sentence 3: why the response works (mirrors reflect all colors equally).
That is a problem → solution structure.
There is only one scientist (not B), no instructions (not C), and no rejection (not D).
key: Label each sentence's job (problem, solution, reason), then match the sequence.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage:
The following text is from an original short story.
Grandmother's roses were famous on our street. Every June, neighbors slowed down to admire them over the fence. But the plant she cared for most was a scraggly lemon tree by the back door, grown from a seed she had carried from the village where she was born.
stem: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It reveals that the plant with the deepest personal meaning to Grandmother is not the one others admire.
It explains why the neighbors admire the roses.
It suggests that Grandmother plans to stop growing roses.
It describes how lemon trees are usually grown.
steps: Sentences 1 and 2 focus on the roses, the plant others admire.
Sentence 3 begins with "But", a contrast.
It reveals the lemon tree as the plant she values most, tied to her birthplace.
So it contrasts public admiration with private meaning.
B, C and D aren't supported: the sentence is about the lemon tree's personal value.
key: A sentence starting with a contrast word usually shifts focus. Ask what it shifts from and to.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: Some critics dismiss video games as mere entertainment. Yet game designers routinely solve problems familiar to architects and novelists: guiding a visitor through a space, controlling the pace at which information is revealed, and making a person's choices feel meaningful. Recognizing these shared challenges, several universities now teach game design alongside architecture and creative writing.
stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that game design involves serious creative challenges that connect it to established fields
To explain how to design a successful video game
To criticize universities for teaching game design
To describe the history of architecture
steps: Sentence 1 gives a view the author disagrees with: games are "mere entertainment."
"Yet" introduces the author's counterpoint: designers solve problems like architects and novelists.
Sentence 3 supports this with universities teaching these subjects together.
So the purpose is to argue that game design is serious creative work linked to other fields.
B (how-to), C (criticism of universities) and D (history) don't match.
key: When a text opens with a view and then says "Yet", the author is usually arguing against that view.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage:
Text 1
Some elementary school teachers believe that assigning homework every night helps young students build good study habits.

Text 2
Studies of young students have found little connection between the amount of homework they do and their later success in school. For these students, free play and reading for enjoyment may be a better use of evening time.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the teachers discussed in Text 1?
choices: By questioning whether nightly homework benefits young students as much as the teachers assume
By agreeing that homework is the best way to build study habits
By recommending more homework for older students
By arguing that young students should not read at home
steps: Text 1: teachers think nightly homework helps young students.
Text 2: research shows little connection between homework and later success, and suggests other activities.
So Text 2's author would doubt the teachers' assumption.
B contradicts Text 2; C (older students) isn't discussed; D contradicts Text 2's support for reading.
key: Find the point where the texts disagree, then predict the response from Text 2's evidence.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage:
Text 1
Urban planners in some cities have widened sidewalks and added bike lanes downtown, arguing that these changes make city centers livelier and better for local businesses.

Text 2
After one city added bike lanes to its main shopping street, many shops reported higher sales, as more people stopped to browse while passing through.
stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: It provides an example that supports the planners' argument.
It challenges the planners' argument with contrary evidence.
It explains how bike lanes are built.
It argues that sidewalks should be narrower.
steps: Text 1's claim: bike lanes and wider sidewalks help downtown businesses.
Text 2: in one city, bike lanes were followed by higher shop sales.
That is a specific case consistent with Text 1's claim.
So Text 2 supports Text 1 with an example.
key: Decide first whether Text 2 supports, challenges or extends Text 1.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage:
Text 1
Many nutrition guides recommend eating breakfast every morning, claiming that it improves concentration during the first hours of the day.

Text 2
In a recent study of adults, researchers found that skipping breakfast did not lower participants' scores on morning attention tests, although those who skipped breakfast reported feeling hungrier.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?
choices: By noting that their study found no drop in adults' morning attention when breakfast was skipped
By agreeing that breakfast clearly improves concentration
By claiming that hunger improves attention
By recommending that adults eat two breakfasts
steps: Text 1 claims breakfast improves morning concentration.
Text 2 found that skipping breakfast did not lower attention scores in adults.
So the researchers would point to their result as evidence against the claim (at least for adults).
B contradicts their finding; C overreaches (hunger didn't help, it just didn't hurt); D is absurd.
key: Base the response on exactly what the study found, no more and no less.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage:
Text 1
A critic argues that the novel's ending is unsatisfying because it leaves the main characters' futures unresolved, denying readers a sense of closure.

Text 2
Another critic contends that the novel's open ending is deliberate. Throughout the book, the characters live with uncertainty about their jobs, their homes, and one another; an ending that tied everything up neatly would betray that experience.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the critic in Text 2 most likely respond to the critic in Text 1?
choices: By arguing that the unresolved ending is an intentional choice that reflects the novel's themes
By agreeing that the ending was a mistake
By suggesting the novel should have been shorter
By claiming that the characters' futures are clearly resolved
steps: Both critics agree the ending is unresolved.
Text 1 sees that as a flaw (no closure).
Text 2 sees it as deliberate, matching the characters' uncertainty throughout the book.
So Text 2 would defend the ending as purposeful.
D contradicts both texts; B and C aren't Text 2's view.
key: Critics can agree on a fact but disagree on its value. Identify which part they disagree about.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage:
Text 1
Some astronomers argue that the search for life beyond Earth should focus on planets in a star's "habitable zone," the range of distances where temperatures allow liquid water to exist on a planet's surface.

Text 2
Liquid water may also exist far outside the habitable zone. Several icy moons of Jupiter and Saturn, warmed by tidal forces from the giant planets they orbit, are thought to hold oceans beneath their frozen crusts.
stem: Based on the texts, the author of Text 2 would most likely suggest that the astronomers in Text 1 ______
choices: may be overlooking places where liquid water could exist outside the habitable zone.
are correct that liquid water exists only in the habitable zone.
should stop searching for liquid water.
have already discovered life on icy moons.
steps: Text 1 focuses the search on the habitable zone because of surface liquid water.
Text 2 points out that water can exist beneath the ice of moons far from the habitable zone.
So Text 2 implies Text 1's focus is too narrow.
B contradicts Text 2; C and D are not stated or implied.
key: When Text 2 adds an exception, it usually implies Text 1's view is incomplete.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: Coral reefs cover less than 1 percent of the ocean floor. ______ they support roughly a quarter of all known marine species.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Nevertheless,
Similarly,
For example,
Therefore,
explanation: A tiny area supporting a huge share of species is a contrast with what you would expect. "Nevertheless" signals that contrast.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Sentence 1: reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor (small).
Sentence 2: they support about a quarter of marine species (huge).
Small area vs. huge importance is a contrast, so you need a contrast transition.
"Nevertheless" signals contrast. "Similarly" (likeness), "For example" (illustration) and "Therefore" (result) do not.
Answer: Nevertheless,
key: Transitions: decide the relationship between the two sentences first.

passage: The first step in the experiment was to measure each plant's height. ______ the researchers recorded the number of leaves on each plant.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Next,
However,
In contrast,
Instead,
explanation: The text describes steps in order: first measuring height, then counting leaves. "Next" signals the following step.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Sentence 1 describes "the first step".
Sentence 2 describes another action in the same experiment.
The relationship is sequence: the step that follows.
"Next" signals sequence. "However", "In contrast" and "Instead" signal opposition, which isn't present.
Answer: Next,
key: Transitions: sequence words for steps in a process.

passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Ada Lovelace (1815–1852) was an English mathematician.
• She wrote detailed notes on Charles Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine.
• Her notes included an algorithm for computing Bernoulli numbers.
• This algorithm is often regarded as one of the first computer programs.
stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of Lovelace's notes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Lovelace's notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine included an algorithm for computing Bernoulli numbers, which is often regarded as one of the first computer programs.
Ada Lovelace was born in 1815 and died in 1852.
Charles Babbage proposed a calculating machine called the Analytical Engine.
Lovelace was an English mathematician who wrote notes about a machine.
explanation: The goal is significance. Only A says what the notes contained and why that matters (one of the first computer programs).
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: The goal: emphasize the significance of Lovelace's notes.
Significance needs (1) what the notes contained and (2) why that matters.
Choice A: the notes contained an algorithm for Bernoulli numbers (content) and it is regarded as one of the first computer programs (significance).
B gives dates only, C is about Babbage, and D is vague. All are true but none shows significance.
Answer: A.
key: Rhetorical Synthesis: pick the choice that achieves the stated goal, not just one that is true.

passage: Some desert plants survive long droughts by storing water in thick, fleshy leaves. ______ certain desert frogs store water in their bladders, drawing on it while they wait underground for rain.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Similarly,
Instead,
However,
As a result,
explanation: Both sentences describe desert organisms storing water in their bodies. The second gives a parallel example, so "Similarly" fits.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Sentence 1: desert plants store water in fleshy leaves.
Sentence 2: desert frogs store water in their bladders.
Both describe desert organisms storing water. The second is a parallel example.
"Similarly" signals a parallel. "Instead" and "However" signal contrast; "As a result" signals cause, and the frogs' behavior isn't caused by the plants'.
Answer: Similarly,
key: Transitions: similarity vs. contrast.

passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 2016, Seattle public high schools moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m.
• Researchers measured students' sleep with wrist monitors before and after the change.
• After the change, students slept a median of 34 minutes more per night.
• Students' median biology grades rose by 4.5 percent.
stem: The student wants to emphasize the effect of the later start time on students' sleep. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: After Seattle high schools moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m., students slept a median of 34 minutes more per night.
Researchers used wrist monitors to measure the sleep of Seattle high school students.
Students' median biology grades rose by 4.5 percent after the change.
In 2016, Seattle public high schools changed their start time.
explanation: The goal is the effect on sleep. A names the change and the measured sleep gain. C is about grades, not sleep.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Goal: emphasize the effect of the later start time on sleep.
Required pieces: the change (7:50 → 8:45) and the sleep result (+34 minutes median).
Choice A includes both.
B is about the method, C is about grades (not sleep) and D mentions the change but not its effect.
Answer: A.
key: Rhetorical Synthesis: match the goal word for word. Here the goal is the effect on sleep.

passage: The committee had hoped the survey would reveal a clear preference among residents. ______ the responses were split almost evenly between the two proposals.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Instead,
Likewise,
Accordingly,
In addition,
explanation: The committee hoped for a clear preference; what happened replaced that hope with an even split. "Instead" introduces an outcome that takes the place of the expected one.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Sentence 1: the committee hoped for a clear preference.
Sentence 2: responses were split almost evenly, the opposite of a clear preference.
The second outcome replaces the hoped-for one.
"Instead" signals replacement. "Likewise" (similar), "Accordingly" (as a result) and "In addition" (adding) don't fit.
Answer: Instead,
key: Transitions: "Instead" introduces what happened in place of what was expected.

passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Mount Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa.
• It is located in Tanzania.
• Its summit is about 5,895 meters above sea level.
• Climbers can reach the summit without technical climbing equipment.
stem: The student wants to identify the country in which Mount Kilimanjaro is located. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Mount Kilimanjaro is located in Tanzania.
Mount Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa.
Mount Kilimanjaro's summit is about 5,895 meters above sea level.
Climbers can reach Kilimanjaro's summit without technical equipment.
steps: The goal: identify the country.
Only one note names a country: Tanzania.
A states it directly.
B, C and D are true but don't answer the goal.
key: Read the goal first, then find the note that matches it exactly.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage:

Honeybees live in colonies.
A worker bee returns to the hive after finding food.
Honeybees perform a movement called the "waggle dance."
steps: The goal: explain how bees share food locations.
A complete explanation needs the dance and what it communicates.
A includes both: the waggle dance, and that its direction and length show direction and distance.
D names the dance but doesn't explain what it communicates.
key: "Explain how" needs the mechanism, not just the name of it.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

Alligators and crocodiles are both large reptiles.
Alligators live mostly in fresh water, while many crocodiles can tolerate salt water.
Crocodiles have V-shaped snouts.

A contrasts both snouts in one sentence with "While."

Katherine Johnson lived from 1918 to 2020.
John Glenn orbited Earth in 1962.
Johnson calculated flight paths for spaceflights.
steps: An introduction for an unfamiliar audience should say who she was and what she did.

passage: Early users found the first version of the app difficult to navigate. ______ the developers interviewed dozens of users and redesigned the menus based on their feedback.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: In response,
Similarly,
For instance,
Nevertheless,
steps: Sentence 1: a problem (the app was hard to navigate).
Sentence 2: the developers acted to fix it.
The relationship is reaction to a problem: "In response."
"Similarly" signals likeness, "For instance" an example, and "Nevertheless" a contrast. None fit.
key: Name the relationship between the sentences (contrast, example, cause, response) before choosing.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: Early reviewers praised the documentary's striking photography. ______ many of them criticized its slow pacing, which they found tedious.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: At the same time,
As a result,
For this reason,
Specifically,
steps: Sentence 1: praise (photography).
Sentence 2: criticism (pacing) from the same reviewers.
Both reactions held together, with a contrast between them: "At the same time."
"As a result" and "For this reason" wrongly suggest the praise caused the criticism; "Specifically" would introduce a detail of the praise.
key: "At the same time" can signal two contrasting things that are both true.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: Urban beekeeping has grown rapidly in many cities. However, researchers studying several European cities found that where hive numbers rose sharply, wild bee populations declined, likely because honeybees compete with wild bees for a limited supply of flowers. The researchers suggest that planting more flowering plants may matter more for urban pollinators than adding hives.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Adding honeybee hives in cities may harm wild bees, so planting more flowers could do more to support pollinators.
Urban beekeeping has made cities better habitats for every kind of pollinator.
Wild bees produce more honey than honeybees in European cities.
Several European cities have banned urban beekeeping.
explanation: The text reports that wild bees declined where hives increased, and ends with the researchers' suggestion that flowers matter more than hives. Choice A combines both points.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Sentence 1: urban beekeeping is growing (background).
Sentence 2: where hives rose sharply, wild bees declined, likely due to competition for flowers (the finding).
Sentence 3: researchers suggest planting flowers may matter more than adding hives (the conclusion).
The best answer must combine the finding and the conclusion. Choice A does both.
Eliminate: B contradicts the finding; C (honey) and D (bans) are never mentioned.
key: Central Idea: the main idea covers the whole text, usually including its conclusion.

passage: A student is writing about an imagined poem titled "Harbor Town" and claims that the speaker portrays the sea as threatening.
stem: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "The grey waves gather like a waiting army at the shore."
"Gulls drift lazily above the sunlit water."
"Children build castles where the tide has gone."
"The harbor lights glow softly in the dusk."
explanation: Comparing the waves to "a waiting army" presents the sea as a threat. The other lines describe calm or pleasant scenes.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Restate the claim: the speaker sees the sea as threatening.
Look for language that suggests danger or menace.
"Waves gather like a waiting army" compares the sea to an army ready to attack, which is a threat.
The other lines describe calm, pleasant or peaceful scenes (lazy gulls, sandcastles, glowing lights).
Answer: "The grey waves gather like a waiting army at the shore."
key: Command of Evidence: the quotation must show the exact quality in the claim, here "threatening".

passage: A city library runs a summer reading program. The table shows the number of participants in three recent years.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the claim that participation increased each year from 2021 to 2023?
choices: Participation rose from 1,240 in 2021 to 1,610 in 2022 and then to 2,050 in 2023.
In 2023, 2,050 people took part in the program.
Participation in 2022 was 1,610.
Participation was 1,240 in 2021, which was lower than in 2023.
explanation: The claim is about every year-to-year step. Only A gives all three values and shows both increases. D compares only 2021 and 2023, which would not rule out a dip in 2022.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: The claim says participation increased each year from 2021 to 2023. That needs two increases: 2021→2022 and 2022→2023.
From the table: 1,240 → 1,610 (up) and 1,610 → 2,050 (up).
Choice A states all three values in order, showing both increases.
B and C give a single year, which proves no trend. D compares only 2021 and 2023, which wouldn't rule out a drop in 2022.
Answer: A.
key: Quantitative Evidence: match the data to every part of the claim.

passage: Archaeologists excavating a coastal site found bones from deep-water fish species that cannot be caught from shore. The site contained no remains of boats, but wooden boats are rarely preserved in the region's acidic soil. Therefore, the absence of boat remains ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: does not necessarily indicate that the site's inhabitants lacked boats.
proves that the inhabitants traded with deep-sea fishers.
shows that the soil at the site was not acidic.
suggests that deep-water fish once lived close to shore.
explanation: Boats are rarely preserved in acidic soil, so finding none is expected even if boats were used. The deep-water fish bones actually hint that they did have boats. So the absence proves nothing.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Fact 1: deep-water fish bones were found. Those fish can't be caught from shore, which hints that the people had boats.
Fact 2: no boat remains were found, but wooden boats rarely survive in this acidic soil.
So missing boats are expected even if boats existed. The absence is not evidence that there were no boats.
Eliminate: nothing mentions trade (B); the text says the soil is acidic (C); nothing suggests the fish lived near shore (D).
Answer: does not necessarily indicate that the inhabitants lacked boats.
key: Inference: complete the logic using only what the text establishes.

passage: A biologist hypothesizes that a species of desert lizard changes color mainly to regulate its body temperature rather than to hide from predators.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the biologist's hypothesis?
choices: The lizards darken in the cool early morning and lighten at midday, whether or not predators are nearby.
The lizards are darker than most other desert lizard species.
The lizards' main predators have poor color vision.
The lizards change color more often during the mating season.
explanation: If color tracks temperature (dark when cool to absorb heat, light when hot) and ignores predators, that directly supports temperature regulation over camouflage. C only weakens camouflage indirectly and says nothing about temperature.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Hypothesis: color change is mainly for temperature, not for hiding from predators.
Strong support would show color changing with temperature AND not with predators.
Choice A: dark in the cool morning (absorbs heat), light at hot midday (reflects heat), and this happens whether or not predators are present. That tests both parts.
C only weakens the predator idea indirectly and says nothing about temperature. B and D are unrelated to the specific claim.
Answer: A.
key: Supporting a hypothesis: the best evidence links the cause in the hypothesis directly to the effect and rules out the alternative.

passage: In a study of 300 hospital patients recovering from the same type of surgery, those whose rooms had a window view of trees had shorter average stays than those whose rooms faced a brick wall. Patients were assigned rooms based on availability, not on their condition. The researchers conclude that the view may have contributed to faster recovery. The fact that rooms were assigned based on availability is important because it ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: makes it less likely that patients with less serious conditions were systematically placed in rooms with tree views.
proves that views of trees cause faster recovery in every patient.
shows that all of the patients had the same medical condition.
means that patients were able to choose their own rooms.
explanation: If rooms had been assigned by condition, healthier patients might have ended up with the view and gone home sooner for that reason. Assignment by availability reduces that alternative explanation. It does not prove causation.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Finding: tree-view patients had shorter stays.
Possible alternative: if healthier patients had been given tree-view rooms, they would leave sooner anyway, and the view would not be the cause.
Assigning rooms by availability (not by condition) makes that alternative less likely.
It does not prove causation (B), does not mean conditions were identical in every way (C) and is the opposite of patients choosing rooms (D).
Answer: A.
key: Inference about study design: ask what alternative explanation the detail rules out.

passage: When the town of Millbrook replaced a parking lot near the river with a small park, several shop owners on Main Street worried that fewer customers would visit. A year later, a survey of those shops found that foot traffic had risen by nearly 20 percent, and many owners said the park now draws families who stop to shop on their way home.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Shop owners' worries about replacing a parking lot with a park proved unfounded, as foot traffic increased.
Parks cost a town more to maintain than parking lots do.
Families in Millbrook prefer shopping in larger cities.
Most shops on Main Street closed after the park opened.
steps: Sentence 1 sets up a worry: losing the parking lot might reduce customers.
Sentence 2 reports what actually happened: foot traffic rose about 20%, and families now stop to shop.
The main idea combines the worry with the outcome that contradicted it.
B (costs), C (larger cities) and D (closures) are not in the text; D contradicts it.
key: The main idea usually links the setup and the outcome, especially when the outcome reverses an expectation.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage:
The following text is from an original short story.
Mara had practiced the piano piece for weeks, yet when she sat down at the recital, her hands felt like someone else's. She glanced at the audience, found her grandfather's steady nod in the third row, and began. The first notes wavered; by the second page, they rang clear.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: A nervous performer gains confidence after seeing a supportive family member.
Mara decides she no longer wants to play the piano.
Mara's grandfather teaches her a difficult new piece.
The audience leaves before Mara finishes playing.
steps: Mara starts out nervous: her hands "felt like someone else's."
She sees her grandfather's "steady nod" and begins.
Her playing changes from wavering to clear, which shows growing confidence.
So the text is about nerves giving way to confidence, helped by family support.
B, C and D describe events that never happen in the text.
key: In literary texts, track how a character changes from beginning to end.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: Ecologists studying a mountain stream noticed that sections shaded by trees stayed several degrees cooler in summer than sections running through open meadows. Trout, which need cold water, were found almost entirely in the shaded sections. The researchers concluded that protecting the trees along the stream may be essential to keeping it habitable for trout as summers grow warmer.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Trees along the stream keep the water cool, which may be crucial for the trout's survival.
Trout prefer meadows to forests.
Mountain streams are warmer than lowland rivers.
Ecologists plan to plant meadows along the stream.
steps: Detail 1: shaded sections are cooler than meadow sections.
Detail 2: trout, which need cold water, live mainly in the shade.
Conclusion: protecting streamside trees may be essential for trout.
A captures the link between trees, cool water and trout survival.
B contradicts the text; C and D are never mentioned.
key: Look for the sentence that pulls the details together. Here it's the researchers' conclusion.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: Historians once described the 19th-century workers at a New England textile mill as passive, accepting long hours without complaint. Recent study of the workers' letters and the town's records, however, reveals that they formed reading groups, petitioned for shorter workdays, and briefly stopped work in protest. These sources point to a far more active workforce than earlier accounts allowed.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: New evidence challenges an earlier view of the mill workers as passive.
The mill workers were satisfied with their long working hours.
Historians agree that 19th-century records are unreliable.
Reading groups were the most common activity in 19th-century towns.
steps: Sentence 1 gives the older view: the workers were passive.
"However" signals a turn: new sources show reading groups, petitions and a protest.
Sentence 3 states the conclusion: the workforce was more active than earlier accounts allowed.
So the main idea is that new evidence overturns the old view.
B repeats the old view the text rejects; C and D are not claims the text makes.
key: Words like "once" and "however" often signal an old view being challenged, and the challenge is the main idea.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: Some scientists argue that octopuses' skill at solving puzzles shows an intelligence comparable to that of many mammals. Others caution that the octopus nervous system is organized so differently, with most of its neurons located in its arms rather than its brain, that such comparisons may be misleading. For these researchers, the more useful question is not how intelligent octopuses are compared with mammals but how their unusual nervous system produces such flexible behavior.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Some researchers argue that octopus intelligence should be studied on its own terms rather than compared with mammals'.
Octopuses are more intelligent than all mammals.
Most of an animal's neurons are always located in its brain.
Octopuses cannot solve puzzles without help.
steps: The text presents two views: one compares octopuses with mammals; the other cautions against it.
The text ends with the second group's preferred question: how the octopus's own system produces flexible behavior.
So the central idea is the call to study octopus intelligence on its own terms.
B overstates; C contradicts the text (octopus neurons are mostly in the arms); D contradicts the puzzle-solving.
key: When a text presents two views and ends by developing one, that view is usually the focus.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: A student tracked how many students biked to school during three months of the spring term. The student claims that more students biked to school in May than in March.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student's claim?

55 students biked to school in April.
42 students biked to school in March.
More students biked in April than in March.
steps: The claim compares May with March.
Evidence must include both of those months.
From the table: March = 42 and May = 61, and 61 > 42.
B and C give one month only; D compares the wrong months.
key: Match the evidence exactly to what the claim compares.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: In an original short story, the narrator waits at a bakery counter for a cake she ordered. A student claims that the narrator is impatient.
stem: Which quotation from the story most effectively illustrates the student's claim?
choices: "I checked the clock for the third time in five minutes and drummed my fingers on the counter."
"The bakery smelled of cinnamon and warm bread."
"A young boy pressed his face to the glass case, admiring the tarts."
"The baker smiled and said my cake would be ready soon."
steps: The claim is about the narrator's impatience.
Evidence should show the narrator acting or feeling impatient.
Checking the clock repeatedly and drumming fingers are classic signs of impatience.
B describes the setting, C describes another character, and D describes the baker.
key: The quotation must show the specific trait in the claim, done by the person the claim is about.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: A researcher hypothesizes that students remember new vocabulary better when they test themselves than when they reread their notes.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researcher's hypothesis?
choices: Students who spent 20 minutes quizzing themselves recalled more words a week later than students who spent 20 minutes rereading their notes.
Most students said they prefer rereading their notes to quizzing themselves.
Students who reread their notes said they felt confident about the words.
Both groups of students studied the same list of 40 words.
steps: The hypothesis compares two methods by how well students remember.
The best support measures memory for both methods under fair conditions (same time).
A does exactly that, and self-testing wins.
B and C measure preferences and feelings, not memory. D describes a setup but gives no result.
key: Strong support measures the outcome named in the hypothesis and compares the groups fairly.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: Maya planted identical tomato plants on both sides of her yard. The plants on the sunny side produced dozens of tomatoes, while the plants on the shaded side produced only a few. Maya concluded that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the amount of sunlight likely affected how many tomatoes the plants produced.
shaded plants grow taller than sunny plants.
tomato plants need very little water.
the plants on the shaded side were a different variety.
steps: The plants were identical, so the variety didn't cause the difference (this rules out D).
The only stated difference is sun versus shade.
The sunny side produced far more tomatoes.
So the logical conclusion is that sunlight affected tomato production.
B and C are about height and water, which the text never mentions.

source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: The city museum usually closes at 5 p.m. On the first Friday of each month, however, it stays open until 9 p.m. for an evening concert. Today is the first Friday of the month, so visitors who arrive at 6 p.m. ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: will be able to enter the museum.
will find the museum closed.
must buy tickets a month in advance.
will miss the concert by one hour.
steps: Normally the museum closes at 5 p.m.
On the first Friday, it stays open until 9 p.m.
Today is the first Friday, so it is open until 9 p.m.
6 p.m. is before 9 p.m., so visitors can enter.
B applies the normal hours by mistake; C and D are not supported.
key: Apply the exception the text gives, not the general rule.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: A bakery began listing the nutritional content of every loaf it sells. Afterward, sales of its whole-wheat bread rose sharply, while sales of its other breads stayed the same. One explanation for this pattern is that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: some customers chose whole-wheat bread after learning about its nutritional content.
the bakery stopped selling its other breads.
customers bought less bread overall after the labels appeared.
whole-wheat bread became cheaper than the other breads.
steps: The change: nutrition labels were added.
The result: only whole-wheat sales rose.
A plausible link: the labels made whole-wheat bread's nutrition visible, and some customers chose it.
B contradicts "other breads stayed the same"; C contradicts rising sales; D introduces price, which the text never mentions.
key: Connect the change described to the specific result, without adding outside information.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: In a laboratory study, bumblebees that received a small sugar reward before a task were quicker to approach an unfamiliar object than bees that received no reward. The researchers note that this resembles optimism in humans. However, they caution that the sugar might simply have given the bees more energy. To tell these explanations apart, the researchers would most likely need to ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: compare rewarded bees with bees given the same energy boost in a form they do not experience as a reward.
give every bee a larger sugar reward.
repeat the study using honeybees instead of bumblebees.
measure how long each bee lives after the study.
steps: There are two explanations: a positive (optimism-like) state, or extra energy.
To separate them, keep energy the same while removing the reward experience.
If bees with energy but no reward behave like the no-reward group, energy alone doesn't explain it.
B keeps both explanations mixed together; C and D don't address the question.
key: To test between two explanations, change one factor while holding the other constant.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: The students in the robotics club ______ their prototype at the regional science fair last spring.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: presented
presents
will present
is presenting
explanation: "Last spring" places the action in the past, so the past tense "presented" is needed.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Find the time marker: "last spring".
"Last spring" is in the past, so the verb must be past tense.
"Presented" is simple past.
"Presents" (present), "will present" (future) and "is presenting" (present progressive) clash with "last spring".
Answer: presented.
key: Verb tense: let time markers decide.

passage: The collection of rare maps, which includes several hand-drawn charts from the 1600s, ______ on display at the city library this month.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: is
are
were
have been
explanation: The subject is "collection" (singular), not "maps" or "charts". "This month" calls for present tense. So: "is".
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Remove the prepositional phrase "of rare maps" and the clause "which includes … 1600s".
What's left: "The collection ______ on display".
"Collection" is singular, so it needs a singular verb.
"This month" calls for present tense. "Is" is singular and present.
Eliminate: "are" and "were" are plural; "have been" is plural and the wrong tense.
key: Subject–verb agreement: strip away phrases and clauses to find the true subject.

passage: The expedition faced severe ______ the team reached the summit two days ahead of schedule.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: weather; nevertheless,
weather, nevertheless,
weather nevertheless,
weather, nevertheless;
explanation: Both parts are independent clauses joined by the adverb "nevertheless". A comma alone creates a comma splice, so a semicolon goes before "nevertheless" and a comma after it.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Check each side. "The expedition faced severe weather" is a complete sentence. "The team reached the summit…" is also a complete sentence.
"Nevertheless" is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction like "but". It cannot join two sentences with just a comma.
Correct pattern: clause; nevertheless, clause.
B creates a comma splice, C is a run-on, and D puts the semicolon in the wrong place.
Answer: weather; nevertheless,
key: Boundaries: two independent clauses joined by a conjunctive adverb need a semicolon (or period) before it.

passage: Each of the orchestras that toured Europe last summer released ______ own recording of the program.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: its
their
they're
it's
explanation: The antecedent is "Each", which is singular, so the singular possessive "its" is correct. "It's" means "it is".
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Find the antecedent: the subject is "Each" (each of the orchestras).
"Each" is always singular, even when followed by "of the + plural noun".
So the possessive pronoun must be singular: "its".
"Their" is plural, "they're" means "they are" and "it's" means "it is".
Answer: its.
key: Pronoun–antecedent agreement: "each" is singular.

passage: Having studied the migration data for years, ______
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: the biologist identified a previously unknown stopover site.
a previously unknown stopover site was identified by the biologist.
the data revealed a previously unknown stopover site.
a previously unknown stopover site became clear to the biologist.
explanation: The opening phrase "Having studied the migration data for years" must describe the noun right after the comma. Only the biologist studied the data, so the sentence must continue with "the biologist".
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Ask who did the action in "Having studied the migration data for years".
Only a person can study data, so here it is the biologist.
The noun right after the comma must be "the biologist".
B and D put "a stopover site" first (a site can't study), and C puts "the data" first (data can't study itself).
Answer: the biologist identified a previously unknown stopover site.
key: Dangling modifiers: an introductory phrase describes the noun right after the comma.

passage: The novelist's two most celebrated works—one set in colonial Lagos, the other in present-day ______ explore questions of belonging and memory.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: London—
London,
London;
London
explanation: The phrase "one set in colonial Lagos, the other in present-day London" is opened with a dash, so it must be closed with a dash before the sentence continues.
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications
steps: Find where the interruption starts: "works—one set in colonial Lagos…" opens with a dash.
The interruption ends after "present-day London".
To close it, use the same mark: a second dash.
Check by removing the interruption: "The novelist's two most celebrated works explore questions of belonging…" is a complete, correct sentence.
Answer: London—
key: Boundaries: paired punctuation must match. A dash opened must be closed with a dash.

passage: The museum's new exhibit opens on ______ it will feature paintings from three different centuries.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: Saturday;
Saturday,
Saturday
Saturday, which
steps: Both sides are complete sentences: "The museum's new exhibit opens on Saturday" and "it will feature paintings…"
Two complete sentences can be joined with a semicolon.
A comma alone is a comma splice; no punctuation is a run-on.
"Saturday, which it will feature" is ungrammatical.
key: Two independent clauses: use a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a conjunction (and, but, so).
source: SAT AIS original item, written to the College Board Digital SAT content specifications

passage: Lena packed three essentials for the ______ water, a trail map, and a rain jacket.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: hike:
hike;
hike, and
hike
steps: The part before the blank is a complete sentence that announces a list ("three essentials").
A colon introduces a list after a complete sentence.
A semicolon needs complete sentences on both sides, and the list isn't one.
"hike, and" and no punctuation don't introduce the list correctly.
key: Use a colon after a complete sentence to introduce a list or explanation.

A dash or semicolon wouldn't match the opening comma; no punctuation leaves it unclosed.
Check: "The marine biologist was invited to speak…" works on its own.
key: Interrupting phrases need matching punctuation on both sides: comma…comma or dash…dash.

passage: Many desert animals are ______ they rest in burrows during the hottest part of the day and become active after sunset.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: nocturnal:
nocturnal,
nocturnal
nocturnal, so,
steps: The first part is a complete sentence: "Many desert animals are nocturnal."
The second part explains what nocturnal means for them, and it's also a complete sentence.
A colon can join two complete sentences when the second explains the first.
A comma alone is a comma splice, no punctuation is a run-on, and "so," with a trailing comma is wrong.
key: A colon can join two independent clauses when the second explains or illustrates the first.

passage: Neither the coach nor the players ______ expecting the storm to cancel the championship game.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: were
was
is
has been
steps: With "neither…nor", the verb agrees with the subject closer to it.
The closer subject is "the players", which is plural.
So the verb must be plural: "were."
"Was", "is" and "has been" are singular.
key: With either/or and neither/nor, match the verb to the nearer subject.

passage: The number of students who signed up for the school's robotics program ______ doubled since last year.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: has
have
are
were
steps: Find the true subject: "The number", which is singular. ("of students who signed up…" describes it.)
"Since last year" calls for present perfect tense.
Singular present perfect is "has doubled."
Note: "A number of students have…" is plural, but "The number…has" is singular.
key: "The number of…" takes a singular verb; "A number of…" takes a plural verb.
